paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.6:3 Relief Claimed See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.6. In Roberts v. Safadi, 2018 ABQB 165, 2018 CarswellAlta 398, the individual Plaintiff sued the Defendants for damages resulting from an alleged assault of the Plaintiff by one of the individual Defendants. The Statement of Claim sought “general damages in the sum of $100,000. All the Defendants were noted in default. A hearing was held to assess the damages to be awarded to the Plaintiff. “A preliminary question for the Court is whether or not the Plaintiff can be awarded more than the amount claimed in the Statement of Claim as general damages.” Justice Mandziuk determined that he was “able to assess the Plaintiff's general damages claim in an amount in excess of the amount claimed in the Statement of Claim.” (paragraph 34) His Lordship said: 25 As a general rule, “the pleadings define the parameters of the dispute and ultimately the court's jurisdiction” and “the commencement document serves as the foundation for the court's jurisdiction” (Shreem Holdings Inc Barr Picard, 2014 ABQB 112 at para 43). In Whiten v Pilot Insurance Co, 2002 SCC 18 (which included inter alia a claim for punitive damages), the Supreme Court of Canada held at paras 87–88: One of the purposes of a statement of claim is to alert the Defendant to the case it has to meet, and if at the end of the day the Defendant is surprised by an award against it that is a multiple of what it thought was the amount in issue, there is an obvious unfairness. … Whether or not a Defendant has in fact been taken by surprise by a weak or defective pleading will have to be decided in the circumstances of a particular case. 26 In the case at bar, the Plaintiff has, on the face of the pleadings, limited his claim for general damages to $100,000. However, the Plaintiff requested $155,000 in general damages in argument. 27 Courts have allowed implicit amendments to pleadings in situations where a cause of action gives rise to an argument that was not raised in the pleadings. … 29 Stevenson and Côté in the Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2017) state in their commentary on page 13–26: The prayer for relief sets a ceiling on the damages which the court may allow, only if the court cannot or will not amend the prayer, and an award of more may be an implicit amendment. 30 In Campbell v Moxness; Co-operative Fire and Casualty Co, Third Party and 3 other actions (1974), 4 AR 123 (SC(AD), aff'd (1976), 64 DLR (3d) 766 (SCC), the Plaintiff asked for general damages in the sum of $10,000 and the Trial Judge awarded $14,000. There had been no application by the Plaintiff to amend the Statement of Claim, and the Defendants argued that the award in excess of the amount pleaded was an error. The Defendants relied on the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Burkhardt v Beder, [1963] SCR 86, which dealt with a stricter rule in the Ontario Rules of Practice in effect at that time, which required an amendment to a pleading if judgment is sought in an amount greater than the amount claimed in the pleading. 31 The Court in Campbell pointed out that while there is a similar rule in Alberta, the context of the rule relates to costs and the determination of the scale of taxable costs: “[i]n this view, the necessity in stating the amount of damages claimed is less vital to the outcome of a trial.” 32 Finally, our Court of Appeal in Jones v Trans America Life Insurance Co of Canada, 1996 ABCA 165 at para 6 stated: “[t]he prayer for relief has little legal status and is not really much of a ceiling”. 33 The general approach may be to restrict the damages award to the amount claimed in the pleadings. However, this is a situation where the Defendants have been noted in default, and a hearing occurred on notice to all Defendants. The Plaintiff's brief in which the $155,000 general damages award is sought was served on all three of the Defendants in compliance with the mode of service specified in the Order of Simpson J dated July 27, 2017 in the case of Safadi, and on the corporate entities at addresses specified in Affidavits of Service. Given this notice, it is reasonable to conclude that the Defendants would not be surprised by the amount sought being in excess of the amount claimed in the Statement of Claim. I do not find that there is any prejudice to the Defendants. In any event, there is no evidence to counter the Plaintiff's evidence that Safadi is the owner, manager, controlling mind, or otherwise closely associated with the two corporate Defendants, and Safadi attended the hearing in person. In Gill v. 1176520 Alberta Ltd, 2020 ABQB 274, 2020 CarswellAlta 732, Justice Feth said: [236] The Rule does not require the amount of punitive damages to be stated or estimated. [237] For most categories of damages, the traditional approach was to restrict the damages award to the amount claimed in the pleadings. See: Staats v CPR (1914), 1914 CanLII 116 (SK CA), 6 WWR 401, 7 Sask LR 184 (Sask SC) at para 9 and Munton v Edmonton (City), 1936 CanLII 405 (AB QB), [1936] 2 WWR 481 at para 21. [238] However, the Alberta Court of Appeal in Campbell et al v Moxness; Co-Operative Fire and Casualty Co, Third Party and 3 Other Actions, [1975] 2 WWR 64, 1974 CanLII 1196 (Alta CA), affirmed by (1976), 1976 CanLII 1268 (SCC), 64 DLR (3d) 766, [1976] 2 WWR 384 (SCC), concluded “the necessity of stating the amount of damages claimed is less vital to the outcome of a trial” and so long as a claim in excess of the amount pleaded does not impair trial fairness, an under-estimated amount in the pleading may be remedied by an amendment application to the trial judge before the judgment roll is settled and entered. [239] The Alberta Court of Appeal subsequently confirmed the reduced significance of the amount claimed in the pleadings, stating in Jones v Trans America Life Insurance Co of Canada, 1996 ABCA 165 at para 6: “[t]he prayer for relief has little legal status and is not really much of a ceiling.” [240] Rule 13.6(2)(c) requires a plaintiff to identify the types of damages being sought, including a claim for punitive damages, but the amounts sought need only be stipulated or estimated for general and special damages, as required by the wording of the Rule. Where a specific amount is pleaded for punitive damages, that may be expressly or implicitly amended by the trial judge. In deciding whether to amend the pleading, the trial judge considers any potential prejudice to the defendant. See for example: Roberts v Safadi, 2018 ABQB 165 at para 33 where an implicit amendment to the pleadings was recognized for under-estimated damages where no prejudice was occasioned on the defendant.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.6:4 Claiming Prejudgment Interest See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.6. In St Isidore Co-Op Limited v. AG Growth International Inc., 2020 ABQB 94, 2020 CarswellAlta 207, 48 C.P.C. (8th) 291, Madam Justice Friesen concluded that “it is necessary for a party to include a request for prejudgment interest in its pleadings”. Her Ladyship said: [8] Section 2(1) of the Judgment Interest Act, RSA c J-1 reads as follows: (1) Where a person obtains a judgment for the payment of money or a judgment that money is owing, the court shall award interest in accordance with this Part from the date the cause of action arose to the date of the judgment [emphasis added]. [9] Despite this apparently mandatory statutory language, the existing jurisprudence including Stoner v Canadian Natural Resources Ltd (1987), 84 AR 381 (QB), 1987 CanLII 3195 [Stoner] and Angle v LaPierre, 2006 ABQB 380 [Angle] holds that in order for judgment interest to be available as a remedy, it must be pled. … [22] I will begin by dealing with the question of whether it is necessary for a party to include a request for prejudgment interest in its pleadings. I find that it is. The Alberta Court of Appeal in Plaza Deli and Gift Shop v Imbrook Properties Ltd, 1992 ABCA 106 (Plaza Deli) adopted and applied the ratio from Stoner on the necessity of pleading prejudgment interest and I am bound by that decision. [23] Furthermore, although the Judgment Interest Act provides that the Court “shall award interest in accordance with [Part 1 of the Act] from the date the cause of action arose to the date of the judgment” (s 2(1)), as D.C. McDonald J observed, “the existence of an absolute right to have judgment for a sum of money does not relieve the plaintiff of the obligation to claim judgment for such a sum” (Stoner at para 11). [24] As for the ostensible contradiction between r 1.3 and 13.6—included in legislation which post-dates both the Stoner and Plaza Deli decisions—while I am not prepared to go so far as to hold that this Court can never grant prejudgment interest if it is not pleaded, this is not an appropriate case to determine that issue. On this point, para 48 of Bard v Canadian Natural Resources, 2016 ABQB 267, is apposite: This Court has the authority to grant any remedy it deems fit, regardless of whether or not a particular remedy has been pleaded … It is with this knowledge that the Court exercises its discretion in allowing new remedies to be pleaded, or not [emphasis added]. [25] While it may theoretically be possible to grant an un-pleaded remedy, the more principled option will typically be to allow the pleadings to be amended, provided the Dow Chemical test is met. Certainly, in cases like the one at bar, where prejudgment interest is omitted in the pleadings due to counsel's inadvertence, it is not appropriate to grant an award of prejudgment interest without an amendment to the pleadings (unless the other party consents to such an award).

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.6:5 Material facts See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.6. 1. Generally … a party must plead all the material facts on which he intends to rely at the trial, otherwise he is not entitled to give evidence of them at the trial. It is clear too, I think, that no averment must be omitted which is essential to success. Wyman v. Vancouver Real Estate Board (1957), 22 W.W.R. 133 at 135 (B.C. C.A.). As to what constitutes material facts, Master Quinn stated: In the context of this application, it is important to note that the rule requires a statement in a summary form of the material facts. In Odgers, Principles of Pleadings and Practice (21st Ed.), page 103, the learned author makes the point that the material facts must be alleged with certainty, and that the amount of detail necessary to ensure precision varies with the nature of each case. They quote the following statement of Cotton, L.J., from Philipps v. Philipps (1878), 4 Q.B.D. 139: What particulars are to be stated must depend on the facts of each case. But in my opinion it is absolutely essential that the pleadings, not to be embarrassing to the defendants, should state those facts which will put the defendants on their guard, and tell them what they will have to meet when the case comes on for trial. At page 103, the learned author himself observes that: The pleader, then, must decide for himself how far it is necessary for him to set out items and go into figures; how far details of time and place and other surrounding circumstances are necessary to make his pleading intelligible and precise. Experience will teach him this; even common sense without experience will help him much, for our law is rapidly degenerating into common sense! Chellew v. Dickie (1988), 93 A.R. 316 at 317 (Master). As to mistaking law for material facts, Master Funduk observed: In Some Notes on Pleadings, J.E. Côté, (1974) XII Alta. L. Rev. 535, the author says, pp. 537–539: It is most unlikely anything in the Revised Statutes of Canada or of Alberta should take the other side by surprise. The only law which should be pleaded in the statement of claim would be regulations or bylaws, private Acts, Acts not repealed but not in the Revised Statutes, or old English Acts still in force, such as the Metropolitan Fires Prevention Act 1774. To plead the Highway Traffic Act or Bills of Exchange Act is almost to insult the intelligence of the court and one's opponents, and might even raise a suspicion whether one does realize that these Acts are well known. Conversely, where one intends to rely upon a statute one must allege sufficient facts. To say ‘The plaintiff will rely upon s. 132 of the Highway Traffic Act’ is useless. It says too much and too little. One should instead give as a particular of negligence: (c) failing to stop in time, or at all, at an intersection marked by a red light alone shown by a traffic control signal facing the defendant. The general remarks given above as to statements of claim and pleadings apply to statements of defence, especially with reference to the desirability of brevity, and the rule against pleading law. Alberta rules 109 and 123 also call for express reference to release, illegality, performance or payment, matters likely to take the plaintiff by surprise, and the Statute of Frauds and limitations statutes. Even in that context, however, there must be sufficient facts pleaded: It is not enough to plead the Statute of Frauds if no one has pleaded facts to show its application. One must at least plead the ‘there is no sufficient memorandum in writing under the Statute of Frauds’. If this defence were based on the argument that the contract was not to be performed within a year, and that fact did not appear from anything contained elsewhere in the statement of claim or statement of defence, then it seems reasonable that it should be alleged in the statement of defence. Just as the statement of claim must give all the facts necessary for a cause of action, a statement of defence must allege all facts necessary for a defence …Ellis v. Ron Carlson Holdings Ltd. (1989), 98 A.R. 32 at 34-35 (Master). And in another case: A plea that a defendant “reserves its rights” to “add to its defence” is a useless plea. It is so because it is irrelevant. Only that which is material should be pleaded; rule 104. There are rules dealing with amendments to pleadings: rules 130-141. That is how “adding to a defence” is to be dealt with. It is unnecessary to plead that a party may later amend its pleading. North West Trust Co. v. Triple Five Corp. (1993), 137 A.R. 323 (Master), at 330, per Master Funduk. And Hunt J. has said: … it is claimed that Liu and the Glowickis breached their fiduciary duties as directors and officers of the company. Second, it is claimed that they breached their duties pursuant to s. 117 of the ABCA [Alberta Business Corporations Act]. It was argued that because these matters were not pleaded (even though the Statement of Claim was once amended), they cannot now be considered. Rule 104 of the Rules of Court states that pleadings shall contain “the material facts” on which a party relies. Rule 109 states that in any pleading subsequent to a statement of claim, a party shall plead specifically any matter …“(b) which, if not specifically pleaded, might take the opposite party by surprise”. According to Stevenson and Côté JJ.A., Civil Procedure Guide (Edmonton, 1992: Juriliber), vol. 1, at p. 320, “One need not plead a general statute like the Fatal Accidents Act if one pleads facts falling within its terms … Public statutes need not be pleaded …” Moreover, in Beelby v. Beelby, [1953] O.W.N. 561 (H.C.), Senior Master Marriott stated at p. 562 that “a party is entitled to raise any point of law available to him at the trial without pleading it”. Novel Energy (North America) Ltd. v. Glowicki (1994), 16 Alta. L.R. (3d) 26 at 69 (Q.B.). Mr. Justice Berger similarly observed: I am of the opinion that the facts giving rise to this economic tort were adequately pleaded by references to the acts of the Caterpillar Defendants. The cause of action itself need not be pleaded provided that the factual situation pleaded discloses the cause of action: Letang v. Cooper, [1965] 1 Q.B. 232 at 234 (C.A.); Bank of Nova Scotia v. Dunphy Leasing Enterprises Ltd. (1987), [51 Alta. L.R. (2d) 324] (Alta. C.A.). Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co. (1994), 17 Alta. L.R. (3d) 251 at 345 (Q.B.). Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co.; was reversed in part [(1996), 41 Alta. L.R. (3d) 217 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1998) 61 Alta. L.R. (3d) 256 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1997) 209 A.R. 400n (S.C.C.)], but the Court of Appeal's decision did not deal with practice issues. In MDI Industrial Sales Ltd. v. McLean (2000), 267 A.R. 394 (Q.B.), Acton J. said, at p. 396: A pleading need only plead the facts which in law would create a certain cause of action. It need not name the cause of action, or name any cause of action, or give a legal conclusion, and may name a different cause of action, or the wrong cause of action: Fullowka v. Whitford (No. 1) (1997), 147 D.L.R. (4th) 531 (N.W.T.C.A.); leave denied [1997] 2 S.C.R. xvi; Canada (Attorney General) v. Becker (1999), 223 A.R. 59 (C.A.). In Al-Ghamdi v. Alberta, 2017 ABQB 684, 2017 CarswellAlta 2447, Justice Goss said: 115 Dealing specifically with an application to strike, in Tottrup v Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection), 2000 ABCA 121, the Court stated at para 11 that it is not sufficient to allege a duty; the claim must allege the facts that support the duty. The Court notes: In my view, it is not the allegation of a duty at law that is critical, but the facts alleged supporting such a duty. For example, a statement of claim alleging only that “A” breached a duty owed to “B” thereby causing damage does not, in my view, disclose a cause of action. Pleadings are allegations of fact and, in my view, where negligence is alleged, that allegation must be supported by facts capable of sustaining a determination that a duty was owed, that an act or omission occurred breaching that duty, and that damages resulted. On a motion to strike it is the allegations of fact that must be examined to determine whether a cause of action exists. 116 The Federal Court of Appeal in Merchant Law Group v Canada (Revenue Agency), 2010 FCA 184, held that the bare assertion of a conclusion is not an allegation of material fact, and further (at para 34): When pleading bad faith or abuse of power, it is not enough to assert, baldly, conclusory phrases such as “deliberately or negligently,”“callous disregard,” or “by fraud and theft did steal”: Zundel v Canada, 2005 FC 1612, 144 A.C.W.S. (3d) 635; Vojic v Canada (M.N.R.), [1987] 2 C.T.C. 203, 87 D.T.C. 5384 (F.C.A.). “The bare assertion of a conclusion upon which the court is called upon to pronounce is not an allegation of material fact”: Canadian Olympic Association v USA Hockey, Inc. (1997), 74 C.P.R. (3d) 348, 72 A.C.W.S. (3d) 346 (F.C.T.D.). Making bald, conclusory allegations without any evidentiary foundation is an abuse of process: AstraZeneca Canada Inc. v Novopharm Limited, 2010 FCA 112 at paragraph 5. 117 The Ontario Supreme Court in Best v Ranking, 2015 ONSC 6269, also held that bare allegations are scandalous and noted that allegations like conspiracy must be pled with particularity (at paras 60-61): A pleading must contain a plaintiff's knowledge of the facts and not merely those facts that he believes or wishes may or may not be true. A plaintiff must clearly plead the facts in support of his claim. Mere bald allegations, without supporting facts or with facts incapable of proof, must not be permitted to proceed. Bare allegations are scandalous and are to be struck out under rule 25.11(b), and allegations of fraud, misrepresentation, negligence and conspiracy must be pleaded with particularity … The opposing party is entitled to have the case against it set out in an intelligible form. (citations omitted)[Ontario's R 25.11(b) is equivalent to Alberta's r 3.68(2)(c)] 118 Similarly in Irwin v Buote, 2016 ABQB 530, Macklin J (at para 43) held: … it is incumbent upon the pleading party to include particulars. A bare allegation of bad faith is inadequate without sufficient facts pleaded in support, and without some particulars (Walton International Group Inc v Rockyview, 2007 ABCA 21 at para 12 citing Tottrup v Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection), 2000 ABCA 121 at para 11). 2. Particularize Regulations, Orders-in-Council, By-laws The law is not to be pleaded … Statutes such as the Motor Transport Act need not be pleaded. However, the alleged facts necessary to give rise to a claim that a particular provision has been breached must be. Mr. Justice Mackenzie in the case of O'Neill v. Rosetown (Town), [1941] 2 W.W.R. 481 (Sask. C.A.), at p. 485 approved of and quoted from Odgers on Pleadings, 12th Edition, p. 86, where the author said: Whenever the alleged claim is the creature of statute being unknown to the common law every fact must be alleged necessary to bring the case within the statute. That case also stands for the proposition that if a specific fact is not set out but if those facts can be properly inferred from other statements made in the pleading, then that is adequate. When one considers regulations, Orders-in-Council and by-laws, etc., it has always been my understanding that the proper practice is as stated by Wilson. J. in Granholm v. Western Canadian Greyhound Lines Ltd. (1952), 6 W.W.R. (N.S.) 562 (B.C. S.C.), at pp. 563–64: It is clear that a pleader need and should not ordinarily cite law whether it be common law or statute law: Boyce v. Whitaker (1779), 1 Douglas 94 at 97, 99 E.R. 65; Partridge v. Strange and Croker (1552), Plowden 77 at 84, 75 E.R. 123. But since the dates of those venerable decisions there has sprung up a whole new body of law made not by the legislature but by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, or by the other persons or bodies to whom the legislature has delegated power to make regulations. This law is not to be found in the statute books. It can be changed overnight by the ruling of the person or body to whom authority has been delegated. I do not think it fits well with the fairness and good sense of our system of pleading to hold that regulations made pursuant to statutes are so much of a piece with the statutes which father them that they, the regulations, need not be pleaded with particularity. On the contrary, I think that a litigant who intends to rely on any of the innumerable regulations and orders-in-council which now constitute such a large proportion of our laws should not only say so but should condescend to particularity in stating exactly what regulations or orders he intends to invoke. It goes without saying that he should also plead the facts which he alleges constitute a violation of the regulation or order cited. The above was adopted by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Anglo-Canadian Timber Products Ltd. v. British Columbia Electric Co. (1960), 31 W.W.R. 604, as well as by Master Funduk of this Court in the case of Kully v. Decore (1981), 34 A.R. 617 (Q.B.), at p. 620 where a number of other cases are also cited … I am of the opinion that if one intends to rely upon specific Orders-in-Council, regulations or by-laws, all made pursuant to the powers granted under public general statutes, they should be particularized and the facts which it is alleged make them applicable and that constitute a breach of their provisions should be pleaded. What Rule Requires of Defendants Rule 104 requires a defendant to set forth the material facts on which he relies for his defence. If the defendant's position is that the representatives are not the representatives of the defendant, that must be expressly pleaded. I therefore find it proper and consistent with the Rules to strike all quotations from the Amended Statement of Claim. Reg.
Generally … a party must plead all the material facts on which he intends to rely at the trial, otherwise he is not entitled to give evidence of them at the trial.
It is clear too, I think, that no averment must be omitted which is essential to success.
Wyman v.
Vancouver Real Estate Board (1957), 22 W.W.R.
As to what constitutes material facts, Master Quinn stated: In the context of this application, it is important to note that the rule requires a statement in a summary form of the material facts.

In Odgers, Principles of Pleadings and Practice (21st Ed.), page 103, the learned author makes the point that the material facts must be alleged with certainty, and that the amount of detail necessary to ensure precision varies with the nature of each case.
They quote the following statement of Cotton, L.J., from Philipps v.
Philipps (1878), 4 Q.B.D.
139: What particulars are to be stated must depend on the facts of each case.

But in my opinion it is absolutely essential that the pleadings, not to be embarrassing to the defendants, should state those facts which will put the defendants on their guard, and tell them what they will have to meet when the case comes on for trial.

At page 103, the learned author himself observes that: The pleader, then, must decide for himself how far it is necessary for him to set out items and go into figures; how far details of time and place and other surrounding circumstances are necessary to make his pleading intelligible and precise.
Experience will teach him this; even common sense without experience will help him much, for our law is rapidly degenerating into common sense!
Chellew v.
Dickie (1988), 93 A.R.
316 at 317 (Master).
As to mistaking law for material facts, Master Funduk observed: In Some Notes on Pleadings, J.E.
Côté, (1974) XII Alta.
L.
Rev.
535, the author says, pp.
537–539: It is most unlikely anything in the Revised Statutes of Canada or of Alberta should take the other side by surprise.

The only law which should be pleaded in the statement of claim would be regulations or bylaws, private Acts, Acts not repealed but not in the Revised Statutes, or old English Acts still in force, such as the Metropolitan Fires Prevention Act 1774.

To plead the Highway Traffic Act or Bills of Exchange Act is almost to insult the intelligence of the court and one's opponents, and might even raise a suspicion whether one does realize that these Acts are well known.
Conversely, where one intends to rely upon a statute one must allege sufficient facts.
To say ‘The plaintiff will rely upon s.
132 of the Highway Traffic Act’ is useless.
It says too much and too little.
One should instead give as a particular of negligence: (c) failing to stop in time, or at all, at an intersection marked by a red light alone shown by a traffic control signal facing the defendant.
The general remarks given above as to statements of claim and pleadings apply to statements of defence, especially with reference to the desirability of brevity, and the rule against pleading law.

One must at least plead the ‘there is no sufficient memorandum in writing under the Statute of Frauds’.

Ron Carlson Holdings Ltd.
32 at 34-35 (Master).

It is so because it is irrelevant.
Only that which is material should be pleaded; rule 104.
There are rules dealing with amendments to pleadings: rules 130-141.

It is unnecessary to plead that a party may later amend its pleading.

Triple Five Corp.
323 (Master), at 330, per Master Funduk.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.6:7 Where condition precedent material See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.6. 1. What is Condition Precedent? The test to identify a condition precedent is set out in Odgers on Pleading and Practice, 20th ed. (1971), at p. 99, as follows: But what is a condition precedent? And how does it differ from the material facts which must be pleaded? Where everything has happened which would at common law prima facie entitle a man to a certain sum of money, or vest in him a certain right of action, and yet in this particular case there is something further to be done, or something more must happen before he is entitled to sue, either by reason of the provisions of some statute, or because the parties have expressly so agreed—this something more is called a condition precedent. It is not of the essence of such a cause of action; but it has been made essential. It is an additional formality superimposed on what otherwise would have been valid. Hence the plaintiff can draft a perfectly good statement of claim without any reference to it; and it is for the defendant to raise the point if he thinks the plaintiff has not performed all that is required of him. If neither party refers to the condition, it will probably be because it has been duly complied with; anyhow its due performance will in that event be presumed. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce Mortgage Corp. v. Manson, [1984] 4 W.W.R. 171 at 175 (Sask. C.A.). 2. — Section 13 Defamation Act Notice There is authority which indicates that a s. 13 notice is a condition precedent so the Defendants must plead lack of notice: rule 108. By failing to do that in the defence that was delivered the Plaintiff is now faced with the limitation period set by s. 13. Getty v. Calgary Herald (1990), 104 A.R. 308 (Master), at 319, per Master Funduk.

Importance of Rule Rule 109 requires a defendant to plead any matter which he alleges makes the claim of the plaintiff not maintainable or which “raises issues of fact” not arising out of the statement of claim. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.6:9 Where malice or fraud alleged See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.6. 1. Requirements of Rule All a litigant need do is plead the “state of mind” to comply with the rule. Often the state of mind of a party is a conclusion to be drawn from the evidence. Conclusions to be drawn from the evidence are a function of the court and this rule avoids the pleader having to draw conclusions. Caskey v. Guardian Insurance Co. of Canada (1994), 148 A.R. 251 at 257 (Master). 2. Where Allegation Is of Bad Faith The Churgins did not plead bad faith or improper motives, despite RR. 113, 115. Churgin v. Calgary (City) (1989), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 97 (C.A.), at 101, per Côté J.A. 3. Standard of Proof An allegation of fraud is a serious matter. The standard of proof for such an allegation has been set out by the Supreme Court of Canada in Dalton Cartage Co. v. Continental Insurance Co., [1982] 1 S.C.R. 164 … The burden of proof is the standard applicable to civil cases which is a balance of probabilities, however, a higher degree of probability would be required with respect to such a serious allegation as fraud. This burden was clearly laid out by Laskin, C.J., at pp. 169–170: Where there is an allegation of conduct that is morally blameworthy or that could have a criminal or penal aspect and the allegation is made in civil litigation, the relevant burden of proof remains proof on a balance of probabilities … There is a necessarily a matter of judgment involved in weighing evidence that goes to the burden of proof, and a trial judge is justified in scrutinizing evidence with greater care if there are serious allegations to be established by the proof that is offered … The case may be proved by a preponderance of probability, but there may be degrees of probability within that standard. The degree depends on the subject matter. A civil court, when considering a charge of fraud, will naturally require a higher degree of probability than that which it would require if considering whether negligence were established. Ye Kiu Trading Ltd. v. Wong (1995), 177 A.R. 247 (Q.B.), at 248-49, per Kenny J. However, in Kowal v. Sun Star Energy Inc., 2020 ABQB 244, 2020 CarswellAlta 684, Justice Woolley suggested that the law has changed. Her Ladyship said: [380] The burden of proof for establishing civil fraud lies on a plaintiff, who must establish the elements of the test for civil fraud on the balance of probabilities. [381] Older Alberta case law, relied upon by the Defendants, said that, given the serious and stigmatizing nature of civil fraud, the standard of proof “must be met by cogent and convincing evidence”: TWT at para 39 (Belzil JA, dissenting on other grounds). [382] The proposition that proof of civil fraud requires a particular type of evidence is cast into doubt by the Supreme Court's decision in F.H. v McDougall, 2008 SCC 53. In that case the Supreme Court emphasized that the burden of proof in all civil cases requires the plaintiff to establish on the evidence that “it is more likely than not that the event occurred”: McDougall at para 44. All cases require serious scrutiny of the evidence, and all require that the evidence be “sufficiently clear convincing and cogent to satisfy the balance of probabilities test”; “it is inappropriate to say that there are legally recognized different levels of scrutiny of the evidence depending upon the seriousness of the case”: McDougall at para 46, 45. [383] The plaintiff must plead fraud specifically; Rule 13.6(3) of the Rules of Court requires that the allegations contain sufficient particulars to allow the defendant to know the case they have to meet. This includes a description of the misrepresentation, who made it, to whom and when: Elliott v Rainbow Homes Ltd, 2018 ABQB 328 at para 4.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.6:10 R. 13.6(3)—Matters which would surprise See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.6. 1. Claims of solicitor-client costs In HSBC Bank Canada v. Lourenco, 2012 ABQB 648, 2012 CarswellAlta 1819, 549 A.R. 25, 72 Alta. L.R. (5th) 389, Madam Justice Goss had before her an application by the successful plaintiff (HSBC) in the action for costs on a solicitor-client basis. In making its claim for solicitor-client costs, HSBC relied on clauses in one of the pledging documents (the Pledge) and in the General Security Agreement (GSA) concerning the payment of legal fees. The question arose as to whether HSBC's pleadings in the action adequately set out a claim for solicitor-client costs. Justice Goss said, at paragraphs 31 and 32: 31 The law is to the effect that where a contract is sufficiently clear, the courts will generally enforce express covenants for solicitor client costs, unless there is misconduct or harshness: Manufacturers Life Insurance Co v Toronto Dominion Bank (1988), 92 A.R. 92, [1989] 1 W.W.R. 474 (CA). Mason J. discussed this general principle in 369413 Alberta Ltd v Pocklington (2000), 79 Alta. L.R. (3d) 222, [2000] A.J. No. 410 (QB): 50 Contractual provisions as to costs are considered in Orkin's The Law of Costs, 2d. ed. (Aurora: Canada Law Book, 1999) at para. 219.1.1. In the context of a mortgagee defending its security, contractual solicitor-client costs are common, and “a contractual right to [such] costs … should generally be ordered”. Orkin also points out, however, that “the right is always subject to the court's discretion, and costs on the lower scale may be ordered”. The court may refuse to enforce the contractual right where there are good reasons—the successful party has engaged in inequitable conduct, or the case presents special circumstances which makes the imposition of solicitor-client costs unfair or unduly onerous: Bossé v. Mastercraft Group Inc., [1995] O.J. No. 884 (C.A.) at para. 65; see also C.D.I.C. v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1989), 68 Alta. L.R. (2d) 194 (C.A.) at 203-04. 32 However, there is some uncertainty in the case law regarding the requirement that a party specifically plead such a covenant. In Laurentian Bank of Canada v Ellacott, 1998 ABCA 382, 228 A.R. 63, the Court of Appeal held that a party seeking solicitor client costs based on a covenant to pay them must actually plead the covenant: 23 The statement of claim on the guarantee does ask for costs “on a Solicitor and Client and Party and Party basis”. But there is no recital of any covenant in any document to pay such costs. So it sounds like a plea for solicitor-client costs is in the court's discretion, which would require misconduct of some kind. Of course no misconduct is suggested here. Counsel for the bank does not ask to amend her pleading, for obvious and very sound tactical reasons. Since Rule 106 and the basic principles of pleading require an averment of a covenant to succeed on it, we cannot say that the trial judge was wrong to give twice column 5 instead of solicitor-client costs. See to the same effect Marianayagam v BM 2000 NWTCA 2. As to HSBC's pleadings regarding costs, her Ladyship said, at paragraphs 39-40, 42–46, 51–52: 39 HSBC relies on the fact that solicitor client costs were included in the prayer for relief in its Statement of Claim. Furthermore, the Pledge and the GSA were entered as exhibits at trial. The intent to rely on covenants in those documents, some of which provide for the payment of costs, was sufficiently clear. 40 Counsel for the defendants in this case indicated that he had no notice that the covenants in question would be relied upon until the morning of the costs hearing. It was argued that the defendants would not presume that the request for solicitor client costs in the prayer for relief was based on the covenants as the successful claims were not claims in debt or for enforcement of security, but for breach of trust and false representation. … 42 The current Rule 13.6 provides that a pleading must include a statement of any matter on which a party intends to rely that may take another party by surprise. This may need to include any covenants in an agreement upon which a party would seek to rely for special types of costs if not doing so may take another party by surprise. Costs, including any known special costs, must now be included in the remedy claimed. Such specific direction did not exist under the old rules where costs did not need to be claimed. 43 The element of surprise is the key consideration in determining whether a statement or matter must be pled. A party must not take another party by surprise. This has also been the concern expressed in some of the case law prior to the changes in the rules. Notice must be given of the intent to seek costs if otherwise there would be surprise. Clearly now, it must be included in the remedy claimed. The greater question is whether the specific covenant upon which a party intends to rely for solicitor client costs must be referenced in the pleadings. In my view, the relevant facts must be recited in the pleadings if a party would otherwise be caught by surprise. To consider whether there would be surprise the court must look at the sophistication of the parties and their negotiating power. 44 In this action, solicitor client costs were included in the prayer for relief in the Statement of Claim. The basis for the claimed entitlement to such costs, a covenant under the GSA, was not specifically pled, although the GSA as a whole was pled and entered as an exhibit at trial. A similar situation existed in Laurentian. In Laurentian the Court of Appeal found that without recital of a covenant as the basis for payment of solicitor client costs in the pleadings, the plea for such costs only in the prayer for relief meant that the award of such costs was in the court's discretion. The Court based its conclusion on Rule 106 and the basic principle of pleading that requires a covenant to be formally asserted to succeed on it. 45 The Laurentian decision, together with many others, were considered by Read J. in Alberta Permit Pro. To reconcile the contradictory lines of Alberta jurisprudence particularly at the Court of Appeal level, the need to give notice to the other side in order to avoid surprise was determined to be key. Pleadings must provide a summary of the facts on which the action will proceed. A party should not be able to suddenly assert a legal right to solicitor client costs where to do so would catch the other side by surprise. However, where no surprise would result from a party to an action not specifically referencing or repeating a covenant or agreement to pay costs on a solicitor and client basis, then reference to the relevant provisions is unnecessary. 46 Late introduction of an argument for solicitor client costs pursuant to a covenant to pay such costs within a proceeding has been found to cause surprise to the other side and is prejudicial. This would particularly apply to unsophisticated litigants inexperienced and unfamiliar with legal proceedings, documents and terminology. This principle would also apply where the clause requiring payment of such costs is included in a standard form agreement and the party sought to be made liable had no input into the negotiation of the terms of that agreement. In such a case, the requirement may be unfamiliar to the party and a surprise occurs when such costs are later claimed. An example of this is where a financial institution attempts to enforce a boilerplate term in a mortgage such as occurred in Laurentian. … 51 As stated in Alberta Permit Pro, to apply as a strict rule that solicitor client costs when claimed under an agreement will never be ordered unless the specific provision of the agreement is pled would be to adopt an extremely formalistic approach to evaluation and application of the substance of pleadings. In my view, such an approach is not inconsistent with Laurentian which confirmed the courts' discretion on costs even where a party is caught by surprise. A covenant which is not expressly pled may in some cases not mandate a particular result, but all of the circumstances in a case may be taken into account by a courts in exercising its discretion on costs. 52 The key is whether a claim for such costs would be a surprise. In this case, I am satisfied that the parties were sophisticated businessmen, assisted by legal counsel in their ongoing dealings as directors and officers of Triple J. It cannot have been a surprise to them that the GSA contained a clause requiring the payment all costs, charges, expenses and legal fees and disbursements (on a solicitor and his own client basis) for enforcement of the GSA and of any other security held by the Bank, and that the Bank intended to rely upon that clause after having pled solicitor client costs as part of their relief in the Statement of Claim. Again, the law generally holds that where parties have agreed to pay costs on a solicitor and client basis, that agreement should generally be acknowledged, accepted and applied by the courts. There are strong policy reasons to enforce a covenant between the parties regarding liability to pay costs on a solicitor client basis when steps must be taken to recover under the agreement. Given the circumstances of the case, I decline to exercise my discretion so as to deny HSBC entitlement to such increased costs specifically agreed to in the GSA by sophisticated businessmen and specifically requested in the prayer for relief in the Statement of Claim.

A party must not take another party by surprise.
This has also been the concern expressed in some of the case law prior to the changes in the rules.
Notice must be given of the intent to seek costs if otherwise there would be surprise.
Clearly now, it must be included in the remedy claimed.
The greater question is whether the specific covenant upon which a party intends to rely for solicitor client costs must be referenced in the pleadings.
In my view, the relevant facts must be recited in the pleadings if a party would otherwise be caught by surprise.
To consider whether there would be surprise the court must look at the sophistication of the parties and their negotiating power.
44 In this action, solicitor client costs were included in the prayer for relief in the Statement of Claim.
The basis for the claimed entitlement to such costs, a covenant under the GSA, was not specifically pled, although the GSA as a whole was pled and entered as an exhibit at trial.
A similar situation existed in Laurentian.

In Laurentian the Court of Appeal found that without recital of a covenant as the basis for payment of solicitor client costs in the pleadings, the plea for such costs only in the prayer for relief meant that the award of such costs was in the court's discretion.
The Court based its conclusion on Rule 106 and the basic principle of pleading that requires a covenant to be formally asserted to succeed on it.
45 The Laurentian decision, together with many others, were considered by Read J. in Alberta Permit Pro.
To reconcile the contradictory lines of Alberta jurisprudence particularly at the Court of Appeal level, the need to give notice to the other side in order to avoid surprise was determined to be key.
Pleadings must provide a summary of the facts on which the action will proceed.
A party should not be able to suddenly assert a legal right to solicitor client costs where to do so would catch the other side by surprise.

However, where no surprise would result from a party to an action not specifically referencing or repeating a covenant or agreement to pay costs on a solicitor and client basis, then reference to the relevant provisions is unnecessary.
46 Late introduction of an argument for solicitor client costs pursuant to a covenant to pay such costs within a proceeding has been found to cause surprise to the other side and is prejudicial.
This would particularly apply to unsophisticated litigants inexperienced and unfamiliar with legal proceedings, documents and terminology.

This principle would also apply where the clause requiring payment of such costs is included in a standard form agreement and the party sought to be made liable had no input into the negotiation of the terms of that agreement.
In such a case, the requirement may be unfamiliar to the party and a surprise occurs when such costs are later claimed.

An example of this is where a financial institution attempts to enforce a boilerplate term in a mortgage such as occurred in Laurentian. … 51 As stated in Alberta Permit Pro, to apply as a strict rule that solicitor client costs when claimed under an agreement will never be ordered unless the specific provision of the agreement is pled would be to adopt an extremely formalistic approach to evaluation and application of the substance of pleadings.
In my view, such an approach is not inconsistent with Laurentian which confirmed the courts' discretion on costs even where a party is caught by surprise.

A covenant which is not expressly pled may in some cases not mandate a particular result, but all of the circumstances in a case may be taken into account by a courts in exercising its discretion on costs.
52 The key is whether a claim for such costs would be a surprise.
In this case, I am satisfied that the parties were sophisticated businessmen, assisted by legal counsel in their ongoing dealings as directors and officers of Triple J.

It cannot have been a surprise to them that the GSA contained a clause requiring the payment all costs, charges, expenses and legal fees and disbursements (on a solicitor and his own client basis) for enforcement of the GSA and of any other security held by the Bank, and that the Bank intended to rely upon that clause after having pled solicitor client costs as part of their relief in the Statement of Claim.
Again, the law generally holds that where parties have agreed to pay costs on a solicitor and client basis, that agreement should generally be acknowledged, accepted and applied by the courts.
There are strong policy reasons to enforce a covenant between the parties regarding liability to pay costs on a solicitor client basis when steps must be taken to recover under the agreement.

Given the circumstances of the case, I decline to exercise my discretion so as to deny HSBC entitlement to such increased costs specifically agreed to in the GSA by sophisticated businessmen and specifically requested in the prayer for relief in the Statement of Claim.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.7:1 Rule 13.7 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.7. Defamation Actions The rule is different for defamation actions: Rule 104 … sets out the general requirements as to the contents of a pleading … However, defamation cases have historically been treated somewhat differently then [sic] other pleadings. The general rule is that the actual defamatory words used must be set out in the statement of claim…Lougheed v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp. (1978), 11 A.R. 55 (Q.B.), at 64-65 (this comment was not reversed by the Court of Appeal at, 15 A.R. 201). In 1021018 Alberta Ltd. v. Bazinet, 2015 ABQB 151, Justice Schutz summarized the law regarding the pleading of particulars in defamation actions: 48 The necessity for care and particularity in pleadings in actions for defamation was considered at length in Lougheed v. Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (1979) 15 AR 201 at 210–219, 3 WWR 334 (Alta SC(AD)) [Lougheed cited to AR]. Where an action in defamation is melded with other allegations relating to different causes of action, these requirements for care and particularity must not be relaxed: Balaz at para 24. On the binding authorities of Lougheed and Balaz, the necessity for care and particularity in the pleadings in actions for defamation is to be strictly applied, and should not be relaxed in situations where defamation allegations are melded with other allegations. 49 Mr. Bazinet also points to r 13.7 to argue that particulars must be provided when defamation is alleged. I agree that particulars must be provided when defamation is alleged. Mr. Bazinet says that the exact nature of the defamation must be particularized, including the words alleged to have been defamatory: Olsen v St. Martin (1982) 32 AR 51 at para 10, 11 ACWS (2d) 412 (ABQB) [Olsen]; Orr v Alook 2013 ABQB 86 at para 4, 557 AR 193. Hughes J has helpfully laid out the requirements for defamation pleadings in Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A. v Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. 2013 ABQB 578 at para 25, 571 AR 284: • Defamation pleadings must contain the details of the publication including the words published by the defendant, the time, place and manner of publication, and to whom the publication was made, so as to provide the defendant with adequate notice of the specific occurrence constituting the wrong. 50 This statement of the requirements echoes Cooper v Hennan 2005 ABQB 709 at para 18, 393 AR 146: • The material facts in a defamation suit must include the publication made by each defendant, the words published by that defendant, which plaintiff was defamed by the publication, the time and place of the publication, the manner of the publication, and to whom the publication was made. 51 Moreover, a pleading falling short of alleging who made what comments alleged to be defamatory, is a fishing expedition: Cooper paras 17–18. I agree. 52 It is clear that there are strict and specific requirements for pleadings in defamation. 53 In this case, Mr. Bazinet must be informed of when, where and how it is that he, not someone else, is alleged to have defamed the Plaintiff. It is not sufficient for the Plaintiff to say that “the particulars are available to Mr. Bazinet, and not the Plaintiff.” Put simply, if the Plaintiff does not know the particular (i) words (ii) that were defamatory, (iii) that referred to the Plaintiff, or what words (iv) were published to a third party, it is logically impossible for Mr. Bazinet to know the case he must meet. Mr. Bazinet is not required to speculate. To paraphrase the Court of Appeal in Westfair: Mr. Bazinet is not required to examine his past life with the Plaintiff with perfect recall, in order to inventory all of his past sins, to see which ones might be relevant. Rather, the Plaintiff must take care to supply proper particulars. 54 Olsen at para 5, speaks to this point: • There is, however, an exception to Rule 106, that exception being where the precise words themselves are material. In such a case it is not sufficient merely to give the purport of the words. Defamation actions are one of the few forms of actions where strictness in pleadings is still insisted on. In a slander action the exact words uttered are a material fact, and accordingly the exact words alleged to have been uttered must be pleaded. It is the utterance of the words which give rise to the action. It is the utterance of the words which is the foundation of the action. 55 Care and particularity require that the exact words alleged to have been uttered must be pleaded because it is the utterance of the words which give rise to the action and it is the utterance of the words which is the foundation of the action. 56 I see no basis upon which I ought to depart from this ratio: “[i]t is settled law that the specific words or passages claimed to be defamatory must be specifically set out in the plaintiff's pleadings …”: Lougheed at 213 citing 11 AR 55 at 65, [1978] 4 WWR 358 (Alta SC(TD)). In Callidus Captial Corporation v. Baumann, 2019 ABQB 120, 2019 CarswellAlta 325 (Master), Master Robertson discussed the requirement that a pleading include particulars of the defamation referred to in the pleading. The learned Master said: [69] There is, arguably, a debate over which decision of the Court of Queen's Bench is more binding upon me, or at least is more applicable to these facts, in connection with the pleading of defamation claims. [70] The defendant relies on Cooper v Hennan, 2005 ABQB 709 (CanLII), an application for particulars in a defamation claim. The Court allowed many of the applications for particulars, but for some of the claims the plaintiffs apparently attempted to rely on the assertion that “the relevant facts are within the defendant's knowledge”. In light of the fact that the former Rules of Court required particulars of pleading in a defamation claim (as do the current Alberta Rules of Court at rule 13.7(f)), the Court directed that the offending non-particularized claims be struck. [71] In the course of her decision, the learned justice distinguished a previous Alberta decision, Rosen v Alberta Motor Assn Insurance Co, 146 A.R. 219 (1993) at para. 11, and declined to follow 550433Alberta Ltd v Stealth Alarm Systems Inc., which I cited above. At paragraph 30 of her decision, the Court did not dismiss the suggestion that there was a “modern test” for pleading defamation claims, but rather she concluded that the plaintiffs were attempting to draw from certain cases “larger principles than [the two cases] permit”. [72] However, the Rosen and Stealth Alarm cases relied on dealt with the requirement that plaintiffs plead “sufficient particularity” to inform the defendants of the case they have to meet. In Cooper, the Court was not dealing with the circumstance where the plaintiffs could not plead the exact words, but where the plaintiffs could not provide particulars at all of certain aspects of their claims. [73] At paragraph 30 she made her view clear about a plaintiff's claim in defamation based on speculation: I thus do not find it sufficient for the plaintiffs to assert that the relevant facts are within the defendant's knowledge so as to suspend the provision of particulars until after examinations for discovery. Such an approach, to me, would encourage speculative lawsuits and fishing expeditions. In my mind, a plaintiff in a defamation suit who does not have reasonable fact information should not sue [Elshat v. Yue, 2003 ABQB 32 (CanLII)]. [74] Accordingly, her decision not to follow Stealth Alarms must be taken in context. She was not deciding that a claim in defamation was bad where the plaintiff could not specifically plead, at the outset, the words used. She found the claim to be bad when the defendant asked for particulars and the plaintiff could provide none. She did not accept the breadth of comments set out in Stealth Alarms, but she did not go so far as to say that a plaintiff cannot sue for defamation where it does not know at the outset precisely what words were used. [75] Furthermore, one reason she gave for not following Stealth Alarms was that it had not been referred to in the seven years since it was decided. The learned Justice seemed to see the decision as an outlier in the world of defamation pleadings. [76] Since then, however, Stealth Alarms has been followed by the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal in Hope v Gourlay, 2015 SKCA 27 (CanLII) at para. 23. This case appears to set out the current state of the law at paragraph 24, after canvassing cases from Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, and Nova Scotia: Given the developments in the case law in Saskatchewan and elsewhere, I conclude that there should be no rule or principle of pleading to the effect that a claim for defamation must be struck simply and only because it does not reproduce verbatim the words alleged to be defamatory. [77] In the end, the overall intent in the Alberta Rules of Court is to ensure that by the time the claim gets to trial, the specific allegations are pled with sufficient particularity. A demand for particulars is specifically contemplated by the Rules. The failure to provide sufficient particulars does not lead to automatic dismissal. [78] In a defamation claim, the requirement that particulars be provided does not justify the dismissal of a claim or the refusal to grant an application to amend so as to achieve that purpose, where the plaintiff has evidence of a prima facie case of defamation in a claim that the defendant has embarked on a campaign to defame it, but the plaintiff is not able, at the outset, to say with detail precisely what was said to whom on every occasion. [79] As with other cases, when each party learns more evidence, it may be necessary to ask for an amendment to ensure that the claim or defence is properly set out in sufficient time for questioning, record disclosure and trial. Master Robertson's decision in Callidus Capital Corporation v. Baumann was quoted with approval by Justice McCarthy in Luan v. ADP Canada Co, 2020 ABQB 387, 2020 CarswellAlta 1362, 65 C.C.E.L. (4th) 57 at paragraphs 219–220.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.7:2 Particulars to be pleaded See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.7. 1. Allegation and Particulars Must Be Pleaded If the suggestion is one of misrepresentation, innocent or otherwise, it is required to be pleaded, along with particulars: Rule 115. Camco Inc. v. Northwind Industrial Ltd. (1982), 36 A.R. 585 (Master), at 596, per Master Funduk. In WIC Premium Television Ltd. v. General Instrument Corp. (1999), 253 A.R. 153 (Q.B.), the plaintiff alleged fraudulent misrepresentation on the part of one of the defendants. In an application for an order striking out those portions of the statement of claim, or in the alternative requiring the provision of particulars, C.P. Clarke, J. said, at pp. 156–157: When asked for particulars the plaintiff responded essentially by saying the information would be the subject matter of discovery. I have been unable to find any Alberta authority that decides what must be provided to satisfy the requirement of rule 115. There is, however, authority from British Columbia and Ontario dealing with a similarly worded rule that gives some guidance. The rule is quoted in the decision of Mr. Justice Greer in Lana International Ltd. v. Menasco Aerospace Ltd. et al. (1996), 28 O.R. (3d) 343 (Gen. Div.), at p. 350 where the court quoting from a decision in British Columbia says the following must be contained in the pleading to satisfy the rule: The pleading, even of innocent misrepresentation, must set out with careful particularity the elements of the misrepresentation relied upon, that is: 1. The alleged misrepresentation itself, 2. When, where, how, by whom and to whom it was made, 3. Its falsity, 4. The inducement, 5. The intention that the plaintiff should rely on it, 6. The alteration by the plaintiff of his or her position relying on the misrepresentation, 7. The resulting loss or damage to the plaintiff. 2. One Cannot Evade Rule by Claiming Privilege Nobody can evade the Rules requirements for proper pleading by claiming privilege. The defendant cannot evade rule 115 by claiming “privilege” for the particulars. That argument if taken to its logical conclusion would mean that in any particular case a party could plead misrepresentations or fraud or the like without any particulars and say that particulars need not be provided because they are privileged. Caskey v. Guardian Insurance Co. of Canada (1994), 148 A.R. 251 (Master), at 260, per Master Funduk. 3. Necessity to Plead Fraud In Pepsi-Cola Canada Inc. v. P.M. Foods Ltd. (1985), 61 A.R. 340 (Q.B.), Lutz J. discussed the requirement that fraud be specifically pleaded. He said at pp. 366–67: In McLean v. Johnston, 3 W.W.R. 913 (B.C. C.A.), Martin, J.A., at p. 917 said: Nothing is more firmly established in pleading than that allegations of fraud must be precisely alleged and conclusively proven (secundum allegata et probata); that is a rule which I have always enforced and shall continue so to do until a higher tribunal corrects me, because it is based upon a fundamental principle of justice: ‘There ought to [be] distinctness and precision,’ as Lord Herschell said in the leading case on the subject, in the House of Lords, Lawrance v. Norreys (Lord) (1890), 15 App. Cas. 210 at p. 211 … and Lords Watson and Macnaghten concurred with him, the former stating, at p. 221: The ordinary rule of pleading applicable to cases of fraud, was thus expressed by Earl Selbourne in Wallingford v. Facts and circumstances must in that case be set forth, and in every genuine claim are capable of being stated, leading to a reasonable inference that the fraud and the injuries complained of stood to each other in the relation of cause and effect. Fraud may be alleged in the largest and most sweeping terms imaginable. What you have to do is, if it be matter of account, to point out a specific error, and bring evidence of that error, and establish it by that evidence. Nobody can be expected to meet a case, and still less to dispose of a case, summarily upon mere allegations of fraud without any definite character being given to those charges by stating the facts upon which they rest. It is also clear that the defendant is not required to seek particulars where as here, the plea is defective, for it does not become effective by seeking its definition… In Stewart v. Bundock (1923), 25 O.W.N. 658, Logie, J., at p. 658 said: Charges of fraud, deceit, and misrepresentation were made in the statement of claim. (3d) 25 (C.A.) the Court of Appeal commented on whether a plaintiff would have to specifically plead misconduct or dishonesty. Bazinet, 2015 ABQB 151, the Plaintiff alleged that the defendant, a former employee of the Plaintiff, had stolen intellectual property from the Plaintiff. In certain limited circumstances, such as in the case at bar, I believe there is sufficient compliance if particulars are delivered as soon as possible after the close of pleadings. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.8:1 Rule 13.8 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.8. See also R. 1.3 1. Duty of the Court It is the practice in a pleading to specify what relief is “claimed”. But that is just a statement by the party as to what relief she thinks might be appropriate. It is not the cause of action or part of the cause of action. That is found in the allegations in the pleading. Relief is just a remedy. The court is required to grant “all remedies whatsoever to which any of the parties thereto may be entitled in respect of any and every legal or equitable claim properly brought forward by them in the proceeding”: s. 8 Judicature Act. The section uses the imperative “shall”: s. 25(2)(e) Interpretation Act. A claim is properly brought forward based on the facts or law pled and if a cause of action is made out the appropriate relief can be granted. Winget v. Safeguard Business Systems Ltd. (1993), 139 A.R. 81 (Master), at 83–84, per Master Funduk. 2. Prayer for Relief Does Not Determine the Cause of Action In K.V.R. Electric Ltd. v. Edgar (1994), 163 A.R. 147 (Master), Master Funduk noted again that the prayer for relief simply sets forth the claim made by the plaintiff based on the cause of action set forth in the pleading. At pp. 148–49, the learned Master said: In the prayer for relief KVR does ask for a money judgment against all the defendants. But the prayer for relief does not determine what cause of action a plaintiff advances. A prayer for relief is only a statement by the plaintiff of what relief it thinks is appropriate for the cause of action advanced. Judgments are based on the cause of action advanced, not on prayers for relief: Wagar v. Little, [1924] 1 W.W.R. 112 (Alta. C.A.); Hoover & Robertson v. Burrows, [1945] 3 W.W.R. 683 (Alta. C.A.); Fedora v. Bayda, [1941] 2 W.W.R. 457 (Sask. C.A.). 3. “Other Relief” Must Be Ancillary to that Claimed It is quite unnecessary for a plaintiff to ask for such further and other relief as the Court may see fit to give because the Court has the power to grant without prayer any further relief to which a plaintiff is entitled, but a plaintiff is only entitled to such further and other relief as is ancillary to the relief specifically claimed. Northwest Co. v. Merland Oil Co., [1936] 2 W.W.R. 577 at 598 (Alta. C.A.).

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.9:1 Rule 13.9 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.9. Willingness to Pay Is Not Enough In E.P. Petroleums Ltd. v. Jack's Transport & Excavating Ltd. (1982), 45 A.R. 344 (Master), at 345, the court held that the following paragraph in a statement of defence did not satisfy then R. 92: 4. The defendant states that it owes to the plaintiff the sum of FOUR THOUSAND DOLLARS ($4,000.00) and the defendant at all times has been willing to pay to the plaintiff the said sum of FOUR THOUSAND DOLLARS ($4,000.00) on the basis that it constitutes a full payment of the outstanding full dispute between the parties. At p. 346 the court stated: In my opinion paragraph 4 of the statement of defence does not amount to a plea of tender before action. Archdekin v. McDonald (1912), 1 W.W.R. 1014, is a Manitoba case in which it was held that a valid tender of money, in the absence of some act or condition which amounts to a waiver, requires something more than a mere willingness to pay, even though expressed, there must be actual production of money. Paragraph 4 does not say that the money was actually tendered, but only that the defendant was ready able and willing to pay it. Even if the case could be treated as one in which there has been a plea of tender before action there is no indication that the funds have been paid into court by the defendant as required by Rule 92.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.12:1 Silence is not an admission See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.12. 1. General The rule must be read in conjunction with other rules. … Rule 119 must be read, firstly, in light of Rules 104 and 109 and, secondly in light of Rule 124 … In Richardson v. Jenkin, 10 P.R. 292, Rose, J., states at p. 294: Rule 148 does not say that every material allegation shall be taken as expressly denied, unless expressly admitted by the pleading of the opposite party, but that silence as to any allegation which, read with rule 128, I take to mean every material allegation, shall not be construed into an implied admission. When therefore, silence is not maintained but an answer given which is insensible if it is not to be read as admitting certain statements in the former pleading, I am of opinion that such statements must be taken as admitted. Barrowman v. Ranchland Asphalt Services Ltd. (1981), 29 A.R. 306 at 324 (Master). And Master Funduk has stated: Silence in a pleading is not an admission of the truth of an allegation in the previous pleading of the opposite party: Rule 119. However, that is a general principle which yields to any particular fact situation specifically addressed by another Rule, as the opening phrase of Rule 119 is “Except as otherwise provided.”Bank of Montreal v. Beacon Industrial Development Corp. (1986), 70 A.R. 218 at 221 (Master). 2. Application of Rule The rule does not apply to those who are noted in default. … when a defendant is noted in default the legal position in Alberta still is that the defendant has admitted the facts alleged in the statement of claim by his failure to deny them… R. 161 [currently R. 119] can only be operative when a statement of defence is filed; it has no application when a defendant fails to defend and is noted in default. Sulef v. Parkin (1966), 57 W.W.R. 236 at 239 (Alta. C.A.). 3. Divorce Proceedings In McKenzie v. McKenzie (2003), 342 A.R. 77 (Alta. Q.B.), Smith J. said, at p. 88: Rule 119 provides that the silence of a pleading as to any allegation contained in the previous pleading of the opposite party shall not be construed as an admission of the truth of the allegation. Rule 119 does not apply to a defendant in default. A defendant in default is deemed to admit the plaintiff's allegations (subject to proving quantum): Sulef v. Parkin (1966), 57 W.W.R. (N.S.) 236 (Alta. C.A.). However, Smith J. then concluded, at p. 89, that Rule 119 does not apply to divorce actions: I conclude that divorce pleadings must be examined to determine whether a fact or an issue is understood to be contested. It follows that not all plaintiffs who fail to defend a counterclaim are deemed to admit the defendant's allegations on default procedure. Further, rule 119 does not apply in divorce matters.

Requirements for all filed documents

paragraphs.text: (1) Every document filed in an action must be in the appropriate form set out in Schedule A to these rules, if any, which may be modified as circumstances require. (2) Whether or not a form is prescribed, each document must begin with the following: (a) the name of the Court; (b) the name of the judicial centre; (c) the names of the parties as determined by subrules (3) and (4); (d) the action number; (e) the nature of the document; (f) an address for service of documents; (g) the name, address and contact information of the party or lawyer of record who prepared the document; (h) once filed, the date the document was filed; (i) anything required by these rules to be included. (3) The names of all the parties must be used in (a) a commencement document, (b) a document that changes any party, (c) an order, judgment or pronouncement of the Court that grants relief, or (d) a document that in the opinion of the person filing the document should contain the names of all the parties. (4) In any document other than those specified in subrule (3), the names of the first 4 parties of any group that contains more than 4 parties may be used, with the remainder being omitted and replaced by the words “and others”. (5) Every document filed and every exhibit to an affidavit must be legible. (6) When a document is filed, the court clerk must retain the original of the document. (7) Authorities referred to in a document provided to the Court must be cited in accordance with rule 14.25(1)(h). Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 24; 85/2016, s. 1(6); 61/2023, s. 2

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.13:1 Rule 13.13 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.13. 1. How to Name a Minister of the Crown as a Party In Apotex Inc. v. Alberta (2003), 35 Alta. L.R. (4th) 134 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Hughes discussed the proper way to name a Minister of the Crown as a party to an action. At pp. 141–142, her Ladyship said: One of the issues considered in Decock v. Alberta[(2000), 79 Alta. L.R. (3d) 11 (Alta. C.A.)] was whether the Minister of Health is a sueable entity. While the court held the Minister of Health is a sueable entity, it said the proper manner of framing the claim pursuant to rule 87(b) is to name the Minister only in a representative capacity: However, pursuant to rule 87(b) of the Alberta Rules of Court, all pleadings shall contain ‘a style of cause setting forth the names … of the defendant … and the capacity in which the plaintiff sues and the defendant is sued, if it is a representative capacity …’. Thus, the only reason for naming an official by his or her office would be to establish that office as representing the Crown. However, pursuant to rule 87(b), the proper manner for framing such claims is to name the officer in his or her representative capacity (i.e., Her Majesty the Queen as represented by the Minister of Health). The public official should not be named, either by title or office, as a defendant. Thus, the ‘Minister of Health’ should not be named as a defendant other than in a representative capacity. At the time of Decock, rule 87(b) read as follows: 87. … (b) a style of cause setting forth the names in full of the plaintiff and of the defendant (but not their residences or occupations) and the capacity in which the plaintiff sues and the defendant is sued, if it is a representative capacity, Rule 87(b) was repealed by Alberta Regulation 109/2001. However, rule 87(b) was re-enacted as rule 5.12(b) by the same regulation. 5.12. … (b) a style of cause setting forth the names in full of the plaintiff and of the defendant (but not their residences or occupations) and the capacity in which the plaintiff sues and the defendant is sued, if it is a representative capacity. As rule 5.12(b) is identical to rule 87(b), it is my view the proper defendant in this case is Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Alberta as represented by the Minister of Health and Wellness. 11. (C.A.), at 344, per Côté J.A.

Endorsements on documents

paragraphs.text: (1) When the court clerk is presented with a commencement document for filing, the court clerk must (a) endorse on the document an action number assigned to the action by the court clerk, and the date that the document is filed, (b) ensure that the document to be filed has endorsed on it the name of the judicial centre where the document is filed, and (c) stamp the document as filed. (2) If a lawyer is acting for a person on whose behalf the action is started, when the court clerk is presented with a commencement document for filing, the court clerk must ensure that the lawyer has endorsed on the document (a) the name and address of the law firm, (b) the name of the lawyer in the law firm in charge of the action, and (c) the lawyer's telephone number. (3) When the court clerk is presented with a statement of defence or a demand for notice for filing, the court clerk must ensure that the document has endorsed on it (a) the name of the person filing the document and, if the person filing the document is a lawyer, the same information as is required under subrule (2)(a) to (c), and (b) the defendant's address for service. (4) When the court clerk is presented with a document that is to be filed in an action after the action has started, the court clerk must (a) endorse on the document the date that the document is filed, and (b) ensure that the document to be filed has endorsed on it (i) the name of the judicial centre at which the document is filed, and (ii) the appropriate action number. (5) If the court clerk is presented with a document that is to be filed after an action has started, the court clerk must also, if a lawyer is acting in respect of the person on whose behalf the document is filed, ensure that the lawyer has endorsed on the document the same information as is required under subrule (2)(a) to (c). (6) When a document is filed, the court clerk must note in the Court file, under the action number assigned to the action by the court clerk, the fact that the document was filed.

Alberta (Human Rights Commission), 2023 ABKB 381, 2023 CarswellAlta 1717, Justice Feth said: [47] Rule 13.15 states that a document is filed when the court clerk of the judicial centre acknowledges on the document that the document is filed in the action. Under Rule 13.14, when the court clerk is “presented” with a commencement document (such as an Originating Application for Judicial Review), the clerk must endorse on the document the action number assigned to the action and stamp the document with the date it is filed. (ii) be endorsed by the court clerk in the following form:
Amended on [date] by [order]
Dated…
and
(c) except as required by this rule, the document or other record must not be otherwise physically altered.

Types of affidavit

paragraphs.text: (1) An affidavit may be sworn (a) on the basis of personal knowledge, or (b) on the basis of information known to the person swearing the affidavit and that person's belief. (2) If an affidavit is sworn on the basis of information and belief, the source of the information must be disclosed in the affidavit. (3) If an affidavit is used in support of an application that may dispose of all or part of a claim, the affidavit must be sworn on the basis of the personal knowledge of the person swearing the affidavit.
